# The adaptive director: a simulation study

*Sword in the Forest (林中剑), milestone M5. Generated by `tools/report.sh`; do not edit
`docs/report.md` by hand. Its text is `analysis/report_template.md`, and every number is
computed by `analysis/evaluate.py` from the simulator's CSV.*

## Summary

The director estimates each player's reaction time from the attacks they face, then sets the
warning (lead) time so they succeed at the rate their challenge setting asks for. We test it on
$players simulated players whose true parameters are known ($runs runs, $attacks_total
attacks in all). It answers four questions from the spec:

| Question | Result |
| --- | --- |
| How fast does it learn a new player? | Median error $err_both_nocal_5 ms after 5 attacks and $err_both_nocal_15 ms after 15. After 15 attacks $w40_both_nocal_15 of players are within 40 ms. The population prior helps for the first few attacks only. A calibration phase would add nothing measurable, so the game has none. |
| Does it hit the chosen challenge? | $on_lognormal_Relaxed_adaptive / $on_lognormal_Standard_adaptive / $on_lognormal_Hard_adaptive of players are within 10 points of the Relaxed / Standard / Hard target, against $on_lognormal_Relaxed_fixed / $on_lognormal_Standard_fixed / $on_lognormal_Hard_fixed with the fixed 420 ms lead. |
| Does it hold up on unfamiliar players? | Yes for faster players ($on_faster_both on target). For slower players $on_slower_both are on target: the slowest $slow_capped_share are limited by the 800 ms lead cap, not by learning. |
| Does it survive a wrong model? | Mostly. With ex-Gaussian bots, $on_exgaussian_Standard_adaptive are on target at Standard. Success is pulled toward the middle (Relaxed $mean_exgaussian_Relaxed_adaptive, Hard $mean_exgaussian_Hard_adaptive), and the 80% interval covers the truth only $eg_cov_60 of the time. |

The fifth question, "does it work on a real person?", needs your play logs and is left for the
playtest.

## Setup

**Players.** A player has a median reaction time $$e^m$$, a log-spread $$s$$ and a lapse rate
$$\lambda$$. The default population has a median of medians of 330 ms (log-sd 0.25, clamped
to 160–850 ms), $$s \sim U(0.12, 0.38)$$ and $$\lambda \sim U(0, 0.10)$$. Each attack, the bot
lapses (no press) with probability $$\lambda$$. Otherwise it presses after a log-normal
reaction time plus a 17 ms input delay, snapped to the next 60 Hz frame. A press up to 400 ms
after the impact is still timed, as in the game; later counts as no press. The test players use
seed 7; the prior was fitted to 20,000 different players (seed 2026).

**Director.** This is the shipped `src/Director` library, unchanged: a 2,976-cell grid
filter, a 3% blur per attack, and control at the target. As in the game, there is no
calibration phase: the director sets the lead from the first attack. A session is 60 attacks
("the run"), and run success is measured over all of them.

**Conditions.**

- *Population prior only*: the shipped prior, never updated.
- *Player data only*: a flat prior over the grid.
- *Both*: the shipped prior plus the player's attacks (what the game does).
- *With calibration* (comparison only): 12 Psi calibration attacks, which choose the lead to
  learn the most, before the 60 control attacks. Earlier builds did this in the tutorial.
- *Fixed timing*: every attack at 420 ms, the designed default of the first slash.

Error is $$|\hat{\text{median}} - \text{median}|$$, using the posterior median of $$e^m$$.

## 1. How fast does it learn a new player?

![Estimate error against attacks seen](figures/fig1_learning.png)

| Median error (ms) after attack | 1 | 5 | 15 | 30 | 60 | Within 40 ms at 15 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Population prior only | $err_prior_1 | $err_prior_5 | $err_prior_15 | $err_prior_30 | $err_prior_60 | $w40_prior_15 |
| Player data only | $err_data_nocal_1 | $err_data_nocal_5 | $err_data_nocal_15 | $err_data_nocal_30 | $err_data_nocal_60 | $w40_data_nocal_15 |
| **Both (shipped)** | $err_both_nocal_1 | $err_both_nocal_5 | $err_both_nocal_15 | $err_both_nocal_30 | $err_both_nocal_60 | $w40_both_nocal_15 |
| Player data only, with calibration | $err_data_cal_1 | $err_data_cal_5 | $err_data_cal_15 | $err_data_cal_30 | $err_data_cal_60 | $w40_data_cal_15 |
| Both, with calibration | $err_both_cal_1 | $err_both_cal_5 | $err_both_cal_15 | $err_both_cal_30 | $err_both_cal_60 | $w40_both_cal_15 |

The prior alone is off by $err_prior_1 ms for the typical player and never improves. That is the
"unseen participant" gap. With the player's own attacks, the error falls to $err_both_nocal_5 ms by attack 5
and $err_both_nocal_15 ms by attack 15, about one 60 Hz frame. The M2 target (40 ms after 15
attacks for 80% of players) is met at $w40_both_nocal_15.

Two findings were not expected:

- **The prior matters only at the start.** It cuts the first-attack error from
  $err_data_nocal_1 to $err_both_nocal_1 ms. By attack 5 the gap is $err_data_nocal_5 against
  $err_both_nocal_5 ms, and by attack 15 the curves overlap.
- **Calibration does not speed up learning here**, which is why the game has none. With and
  without 12 Psi attacks first, the curves are the same within noise (fig. 1, right). The reason is the evidence. The game times every press up
  to 400 ms after the impact, so almost every attack yields an exact reaction time, whatever the
  lead. The lead only decides where the press is censored. Psi's careful choice of lead buys
  information that a timed press already gives for free. It would matter if only success or
  failure were observed. So the tutorial spends its attacks on teaching, and the director
  controls from the first one.

The estimate is honest about its doubt. The 80% interval holds the true median for
$cov_both_nocal_15 of players at attack 15 and $cov_both_nocal_60 at attack 60. It is slightly
conservative late on, because the per-attack blur keeps it wide enough to follow a player who
changes.

## 2. Does it hit the chosen challenge?

![Success rate per player](figures/fig2_success.png)

| Challenge (target) | Adaptive: on target ±10 | Adaptive: mean (SD) | Fixed 420 ms: on target | Fixed: mean (SD) | Binomial SD floor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Relaxed (0.85) | $on_lognormal_Relaxed_adaptive | $mean_lognormal_Relaxed_adaptive ($sd_lognormal_Relaxed_adaptive) | $on_lognormal_Relaxed_fixed | $mean_lognormal_Relaxed_fixed ($sd_lognormal_Relaxed_fixed) | $floor_Relaxed |
| Standard (0.70) | $on_lognormal_Standard_adaptive | $mean_lognormal_Standard_adaptive ($sd_lognormal_Standard_adaptive) | $on_lognormal_Standard_fixed | $mean_lognormal_Standard_fixed ($sd_lognormal_Standard_fixed) | $floor_Standard |
| Hard (0.55) | $on_lognormal_Hard_adaptive | $mean_lognormal_Hard_adaptive ($sd_lognormal_Hard_adaptive) | $on_lognormal_Hard_fixed | $mean_lognormal_Hard_fixed ($sd_lognormal_Hard_fixed) | $floor_Hard |

A fixed lead is right for nobody in particular. It ranges from trivial for fast players to
nearly impossible for slow ones (SD $sd_lognormal_Standard_fixed). Adaptive timing puts nearly
everyone in the band. Its spread matches the binomial floor: the noise you get from 60 coin
flips at exactly the target. So almost all the variation left is luck, not mistuning.

The prior alone gets the *average* right ($mean_default_prior at Standard), but only
$on_default_prior of individual players are on target. Personal data, not the prior, makes
the challenge fair.

![The lead the director settles on](figures/fig5_leads.png)

Fig. 5 shows how. The control lead grows almost linearly with the true median. The spread at a
given median comes from the player's spread and lapse rate: an erratic player needs a longer
lead to succeed 70% of the time. The two clamps show at the ends. The fastest players
(population clamped at 160 ms) sit on the 200 ms floor and get it slightly easy. The slowest sit
on the 800 ms cap (section 3).

## 3. Does it hold up on unfamiliar players?

The prior stays the one fitted to the default population. The test players are drawn from the
same population with every median scaled by 0.75 (median of medians ≈ 250 ms) or by 1.4
(≈ 460 ms). Each player keeps its z-score, so the three populations are paired.

![Error on shifted populations](figures/fig3_shifted.png)

| Population | Prior only: error | Both: error at 15 / 60 | Within 40 ms at 15 | On target (Standard): adaptive | Fixed 420 ms |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Faster (×0.75) | $err_faster_prior_15 ms | $err_faster_both_nocal_15 / $err_faster_both_nocal_60 ms | $w40_faster_both_nocal_15 | $on_faster_both (mean $mean_faster_both) | $on_faster_fixed (mean $mean_faster_fixed) |
| Default | $err_default_prior_15 ms | $err_default_both_nocal_15 / $err_default_both_nocal_60 ms | $w40_default_both_nocal_15 | $on_default_both (mean $mean_default_both) | $on_default_fixed (mean $mean_default_fixed) |
| Slower (×1.4) | $err_slower_prior_15 ms | $err_slower_both_nocal_15 / $err_slower_both_nocal_60 ms | $w40_slower_both_nocal_15 | $on_slower_both (mean $mean_slower_both) | $on_slower_fixed (mean $mean_slower_fixed) |

A wrong prior costs a few attacks, not the session. On the slower population the prior
starts far off and pulls the first estimates toward 330 ms. The shipped director then trails
the flat prior for the first handful of attacks, and catches up by about attack 10. At attack
15, $w40_slower_both_nocal_15 are within 40 ms, below the 80% bar the default population meets.
But the error keeps falling, to $err_slower_both_nocal_60 ms by attack 60. The 2% floor in the
prior is what makes this recovery possible. The faster population is learned *faster* than the
default one, because short reaction times are less noisy in milliseconds. With no calibration phase, though,
the first attacks count toward the run. For faster players the prior's first guess is too slow,
so the opening attacks are easy, and their mean success ends a little high ($mean_faster_both
against 0.70).

The remaining gap at the slow end is a design limit, not an estimation error. Leads stop at
800 ms. A player whose median is above about $slow_capped_min_median ms cannot reach 70% at
any lead the game allows. That is $slow_capped_share of the slower population, with a mean
success of $slow_capped_mean_success. Without them, $slow_uncapped_on of slower players are on
target.

## 4. Does it survive a wrong model?

Real reaction times are often better described by an ex-Gaussian: a normal $$(\mu, \sigma)$$
plus an exponential tail $$\tau$$. It is sharper on the fast side and heavier on the slow side
than a log-normal with the same median. Each bot here keeps a default-population player's median and lapse rate. It
draws $$\sigma$$ as 6–15% of the median and $$\tau$$ as 20–50% of it (median $$\tau$$/median
$eg_tau_share), then solves for $$\mu$$ so the median is unchanged.

![A wrong model](figures/fig4_wrong_model.png)

| Challenge (target) | Ex-Gaussian: on target | Mean (SD) | Fixed 420 ms: on target | Log-normal: mean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Relaxed (0.85) | $on_exgaussian_Relaxed_adaptive | $mean_exgaussian_Relaxed_adaptive ($sd_exgaussian_Relaxed_adaptive) | $on_exgaussian_Relaxed_fixed | $mean_lognormal_Relaxed_adaptive |
| Standard (0.70) | $on_exgaussian_Standard_adaptive | $mean_exgaussian_Standard_adaptive ($sd_exgaussian_Standard_adaptive) | $on_exgaussian_Standard_fixed | $mean_lognormal_Standard_adaptive |
| Hard (0.55) | $on_exgaussian_Hard_adaptive | $mean_exgaussian_Hard_adaptive ($sd_exgaussian_Hard_adaptive) | $on_exgaussian_Hard_fixed | $mean_lognormal_Hard_adaptive |

The director still works, and it fails gracefully. Averaged over all attacks, its predictions
stay close to what happens. The weighted gap between predicted and observed success is
$ece_exgaussian points, against $ece_lognormal for log-normal bots. But the misfit has a
direction. Success is pulled toward the middle:

- **Relaxed is too hard:** mean $mean_exgaussian_Relaxed_adaptive against 0.85.
- **Hard is too easy:** mean $mean_exgaussian_Hard_adaptive against 0.55.
- **Standard is right:** mean $mean_exgaussian_Standard_adaptive.

The cause is the finding from section 1. Almost every press is timed, whatever the lead, so the
filter fits a log-normal to the player's *whole* reaction-time distribution, not just to the
part near the leads it uses. The best overall log-normal matches the ex-Gaussian in the bulk,
near the median and Standard's leads. Its success curve is steeper than the true one further
out. Above the bulk, the long exponential tail holds more slow presses than the fit expects,
so long (Relaxed) leads succeed less often than predicted. Below it, short (Hard) leads succeed
more often.

The median estimate is biased by $eg_bias_median ms (median, after 60 attacks). Its 80%
interval covers the truth only $eg_cov_60 of the time, because the filter is confident in a
model that is not quite right. In play this means the three challenge settings are a little
closer together than their labels say. For a real person, the logs will show whether this
matters. If it does, the cheapest fix is a third shape parameter, or a per-challenge offset
learned from the predicted-against-observed record the F2 overlay already keeps.

## Limits and next steps

- **Every player here is a bot.** The model's real test is your play logs: the fifth question.
  The prior should be refit from them, as the spec plans.
- **Players don't change during a session here.** The blur exists for players who improve or
  tire; a drifting-player experiment would test it.
- **One distribution covers deflects and rolls.** Red attacks may need their own offset.
- **The lead cap (800 ms) is a design choice.** Section 3 shows its cost for very slow
  players: $slow_capped_share of a population 40% slower than ours. Raising it, or letting very slow
  players fall back to a lower target, is a playtest question.
- **Calibration.** It does not speed up learning when presses are timed (section 1), so the
  game ships without it. If real players' presses turn out less clean than a bot's (mashing,
  hesitating), the comparison arm is the place to check whether it should come back.

## Reproduce

```bash
tools/report.sh
```

It runs the simulator (`dotnet run --project sim -c Release -- --study m5`, about 30 s), writes
the CSV to `analysis/out/`, and then runs `analysis/evaluate.py`. That script draws
`docs/figures/*.png` and fills this template into `docs/report.md`. Everything is seeded, so a
rerun gives the same numbers.
